newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ATHLETICS-THUGWANE RUNS ON DESPITE ASSAULTS AND THREATS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-THUGWANE RUNS ON DESPITE ASSAULTS AND THREATS.

text.p: Since becoming the first black South African to win Olympic gold, Josia Thugwane has been assaulted, his life threatened and his career potentially derailed by a succession of trainers.
Now, against all the odds, the diminutive 26-year-old, a former cattle herdboy, believes he is back on track after months of ordeals.
Only five months before his surprise win in Atlanta last year, Thugwane was shot in the face by a car hijacker.
Following the Games, he was hardly back home at his shack in an impoverished township 200 km east of Johannesburg when he found fame had cost him the uneventful life he craved.

Thugwane fled two homes after a local gang -- probably, he thinks, the same people who hijacked him -- threatened to kill him, his wife and two small daughters. He believes jealousy was a likely motive.
He was also hounded by agents out for a quick buck and by journalists caught up in a media frenzy.

"Now everything has calmed down, and I'm very happy. I have a good agent who channels everything properly," he said at his comfortable new home in a quiet middle-class suburb in Middelburg, bought for him by the coal mining company where he works part-time as a security guard.
The move has helped raise his morale, undampened by an assault last week from an irate motorist.
Relaxing in his lounge adorned by modern furnishings mixed with carved African woodwork and trophies from his sporting triumphs, Thugwane explains in his native Ndebele how he enjoys his new life.

"Now I can quietly go to the shop without being bothered," he said, adding that he has befriended his white neighbours in the suburb which only a few years ago banned black residents under apartheid laws.
A few months ago, under all the pressures, he was full of doubt. "It seems as if maybe what I've done I might not be able to do again," he said. But now his fears have dissipated.
"I can train quietly again without anyone bothering me and without worrying that someone will attack me," said an athlete who once trained with daily jogs up and down mine dumps.
Thugwane is determined to stick to a recipe that has self-evidently been successful.
"After winning the gold medal, trainers did try to tell me how to train, but I didn't like it. I won all my races and the gold medal by training myself and I will still do the same."
Whether he has made the right decision will be tested when Thugwane runs in his first major appearance since his Atlanta win in the London marathon on April 13.
"Given the nature of the London course I believe Thugwane could pose a real threat to the long-standing record of two hours eight minutes 16 seconds," race coordinator Dave Bedford said.

A poster in Thugwane's home picturing South Africa's first black president Nelson Mandela, against the bright colours of the new flag, remains a poignant reminder of his words after he won the Olympic title.
"This medal is for a very special man, President Mandela. I was running for the president. I was running for my country, my country."
